titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Minaya brings the king a gift; royal favour; the Infantes plan the marriages (tiradas 96–101, lines 1799–1884)
part: Tiradas 96–101 · Minaya brings the king a gift; royal favour; the Infantes plan the marriages (lines 1799–1884)

sentences.t:
Alegres son por Valençia las yentes cristianas,
tantos avien de averes, de cavallos e de armas;
sentences.l:
Glad are through Valençia the people Christian,
so-many they-had of goods, of horses and of arms;
sentences.i: Glad are the Christian folk throughout Valencia, so much wealth they had, so many horses and arms;
sentences.n: Tirada 96 (assonance á-a) — The Christians rejoice; the Çid sends the king a new present (Pidal: Gozo de los cristianos. — El Cid envía nuevo presente al rey). The line-ends run cristianas, armas, amas, casadas, nada: stressed á, then a, a fresh assonance after the á-o of tirada 95. por Valençia, 'through Valencia', all over the city. yentes = gentes. avien, imperfect of aver in -ie (= habían), aver as a full verb, 'to have, hold'. averes, 'goods, wealth' (aver as a noun).

sentences.t:
alegre es doña Ximena e sus fijas amas,
e todas la[s] otras dueñas que[s] tienen por casadas.
sentences.l:
glad is doña Ximena and her daughters both,
and all the other ladies who-themselves hold for married.
sentences.i: glad is Doña Ximena, and both her daughters, and all the other ladies, who count themselves as good as married.
sentences.n: amas = ambas, 'both'. la[s] and the s of que[s] are Pidal's (in italics). que[s] = que se: the ladies se tienen por casadas, 'hold themselves married', on the strength of the Çid's promise in tirada 95 (vv. 1765–66) to marry them to his vassals with a dowry of two hundred marks apiece.

sentences.i: The good Çid lost no time at all: “Where are you, my worthy friend? Come here, Minaya. For what fell to your own share you owe no thanks to anyone;
sentences.n: El bueno de mio Çid, 'the good one of my Çid', the good Çid. non lo tardó por nada, 'did not delay it for anything', with the double negative. Do = 'where' (Latin de ubi). caboso, 'accomplished, worthy'; Pidal's note: a term of praise, as at v. 226. ca[d]ió, preterite of caer, 'fell (to you as your share)', the d Pidal's (in italics), as in ca[d]ié at v. 1796. vos non gradeçedes nada is uncertain: most likely 'you owe thanks to no one for it', that is, your share is yours by right and no favour, and so the Çid now offers a gift on top of it; it might also mean 'you set no store by it', you think it little. The first reading fits the poem's other use of gradeçer with a: e él non gelo gradeçe sinon a Jesu Cristo, 'and he owes thanks for it to none but Jesus Christ' (v. 1624). The verse is not glossed by Pidal.

sentences.t:
desta mi quinta, dígovos sin falla,
prended lo que quisiéredes, lo otro remanga.
sentences.l:
of-this my fifth, I-tell-you without fail,
take that which you-may-wish, the other let-remain.
sentences.i: of this fifth of mine, I tell you truly, take what you will, and let the rest remain.
sentences.n: quinta, the Çid's fifth of the spoil, the leader's share. dígovos = digo vos, 'I tell you', the pronoun glued on after the verb. sin falla, 'without fail', a hemistich filler. prended, imperative of prender, 'take'. quisiéredes, future subjunctive of querer, 'you may wish'. Pidal's note: remanga, 'quede', 'let it remain', present subjunctive of remanir (compare remanida, v. 281, and remanidas, v. 1308).

sentences.l:
And tomorrow at the morning to-go you-will without fail
with horses of-this fifth that I have won,
with saddles and with bridles and with a-sword-each,
sentences.i: And tomorrow morning you shall set out without fail, with horses from this fifth that I have won, with saddles and bridles and a sword on each,
sentences.n: cras, 'tomorrow' (Latin cras); ha la mañana, 'in the morning', ha a spelling of the preposition a. ir vos hedes, the split future, 'you will go' (= os iréis): the infinitive, the pronoun, then hedes (= habéis). ganada agrees with quinta, the participle after aver still agreeing with its object. señas espadas, 'a sword apiece' (señas, distributive, 'one each'). Pidal compares v. 818, where the first gift of thirty horses went to the king saddled and bridled, each with a sword hanging from the saddle-bow.

sentences.t:
por amor de mi mugier e de mis fijas amas,
por que assí las enbió dond ellas son pagadas,
estos dozientos cavallos irán en presentajas,
que non díga mal el rey Alfons del que Valençia manda.”
sentences.l:
for love of my wife and of my daughters both,
because thus them he-sent where they are content,
these two-hundred horses will-go in gifts,
that not may-say ill the king Alfons of-him who Valençia rules.”
sentences.i: for love of my wife and of both my daughters, because he sent them on, as he did, to where they are content, these two hundred horses shall go to him as gifts, so that King Alfonso may speak no ill of him who rules Valencia.”
sentences.n: por amor de, 'for the sake of'. las enbió, 'he sent them', the king the subject: Alfonso let Ximena and the daughters leave Castile for Valencia (vv. 1350–66, tirada 82). dond = donde. pagadas, 'satisfied, content' (pagar, 'to please, satisfy'). presentajas, 'gifts, presents'. Pidal's note to v. 1813: on the king's fifth of the captured horses, which the Çid sends him, see his introduction, p. 99. que non díga, purpose with the subjunctive, 'so that he may not say'. del que Valençia manda, 'of him who rules Valencia', the Çid speaking of himself in the third person.

sentences.t: Mandó a Per Vermu[doz] que f[o]sse con Minaya.
sentences.l: He-ordered to Per Vermu[doz] that he-[s]hould-go with Minaya.
sentences.i: He ordered Per Vermudoz to go with Minaya.
sentences.n: Per Vermu[doz], who carried the Çid's banner in the battle at Alcocer (vv. 689–712, tirada 34), the ending Pidal's (in italics). a marks the personal object. f[o]sse = fuesse, imperfect subjunctive of ir (borrowed from ser), the o Pidal's (in italics).

sentences.t:
Otro dia mañana privado cavalgavan,
e dozientos omnes lievan en su conpaña,
sentences.l:
Next day morning quickly they-were-riding,
and two-hundred men they-take in their company,
sentences.i: Early the next morning they were quickly in the saddle, taking two hundred men in their company,
sentences.n: Otro dia mañana, 'the next day in the morning'. privado, 'quickly, at once' (an adverb). cavalgavan, imperfect beside the present lievan: epic tense-mixing. omnes = hombres. lievan = llevan, 'they take'. conpaña, 'company'.

sentences.t:
con saludes del Çid que las manos le besava:
desta lid que [mio Çid] ha arrancada
dozientos cavallos le enbiava en presentaja,
“e servir lo he sienpre mientra que ovisse el alma.”
sentences.l:
with greetings from-the Çid who the hands to-him was-kissing:
of-this battle that [my Çid] has won
two-hundred horses to-him he-was-sending in gift,
“and serve him I-will always while that I-should-have the soul.”
sentences.i: with greetings from the Çid, who kissed his hands: from this battle that my Çid has won he was sending him two hundred horses as a gift — “and I will serve him always, as long as there is breath in me.”
sentences.n: que las manos le besava, 'who kissed his hands', the message formula of homage (as at v. 1322). [mio Çid] is Pidal's (in italics). arrancada, 'won' (arrancar, 'to rout'), agreeing with lid. Pidal numbers this line 1819b. The last verse slips from reported message into the Çid's own words. servir lo he, split future, 'I will serve him' (= le serviré). mientra que, 'while'. Pidal's note: ovisse, a dialect form for oviesse, imperfect subjunctive of aver (compare sovisse, v. 1788). el alma, 'the soul', the breath of life: 'as long as I live'.

sentences.t:
Salidos son de Valençia e pienssan de andar,
tales ganancias traen que son a aguardar.
sentences.l:
Gone-out are-they from Valençia and they-think to travel,
such gains they-bring that they-are to guard.
sentences.i: They have gone out from Valencia and set off on their way; such riches they carry that they need close guarding.
sentences.n: Tirada 97 (assonance á) — Minaya takes the present to Castile (Pidal: Minaya lleva el presente a Castilla). The line-ends andar, aguardar, dan, preguntar carry a stressed á; parte (v. 1824) counts with them, its unstressed last syllable disregarded. Salidos son, ser + participle with a verb of motion. pienssan de andar, 'they set about travelling' (penssar de + infinitive, 'to set about'). ganancias, spelled here with plain c (ganançias elsewhere). son a aguardar, 'are to be guarded', ser a + infinitive.

sentences.t:
Andan los días e las noches, [que vagar non se dan]
e passada han la sierra, que las otras tierras parte.
sentences.l:
They-go the days and the nights, [for rest not themselves they-give]
and crossed they-have the sierra, which the other lands divides.
sentences.i: They ride day and night, giving themselves no rest, and they have crossed the sierra that marks off the lands beyond.
sentences.n: Andan los días e las noches, 'they travel the days and the nights', the time as a direct object. The second half of v. 1823, que vagar non se dan, is wholly Pidal's (in italics), the formula of vv. 434 and 650; vagar, 'leisure, rest'. passada han la sierra, aver + participle agreeing with its object (passada, la sierra). parte, 'divides' (partir). Pidal's note: the sierra that separates the basin of the Tajo from that of the Duero; here the Guadarrama. las otras tierras, 'the other lands', those beyond, Castile.

sentences.t: Por el rey don Alfons tómanse a preguntar.
sentences.l: For the king don Alfons they-take-themselves to ask.
sentences.i: They begin to ask after King Alfonso.
sentences.n: Por … preguntar, 'to ask after'. tómanse a preguntar, 'they set themselves to ask', tomarse a + infinitive, 'to begin to'.

sentences.t:
Passando van las sierras e los montes e las aguas,
llegan a Valladolid do el rey Alfons estava;
sentences.l:
Passing they-go the sierras and the mountains and the waters,
they-arrive at Valladolid where the king Alfons was;
sentences.i: On they go, over the sierras and the mountains and the rivers, and they reach Valladolid, where King Alfonso was.
sentences.n: Tirada 98 (assonance á-a) — Minaya reaches Valladolid (Pidal: Minaya llega a Valladolid). The line-ends aguas, estava, Minaya, conpaña, presentaja go back to stressed á, then a. Passando van, ir + gerund, 'they go passing'. montes, 'mountains, wooded uplands'; aguas, 'waters', the rivers. do = 'where'. Valladolid, on the Pisuerga in Old Castile, where the court now is.

sentences.t:
enviávale mandado Per Vermu[doz] e Minaya,
que mandasse reçebir a esta conpaña
mio Çid el de Valençia enbía su[e] presentaja.
sentences.l:
sent-to-him message Per Vermu[doz] and Minaya,
that he-should-order to-receive to this company:
my Çid he of Valençia sends hi[s] gift.
sentences.i: Per Vermudoz and Minaya sent word to him, asking him to have this company received: my Çid, the lord of Valencia, was sending him a gift.
sentences.n: enviávale, imperfect singular with two subjects, 'sent him'. mandado, 'message, word'. que mandasse reçebir a esta conpaña, 'that he should order (someone) to receive this company', the infinitive with no subject expressed; a marks the personal object. The last verse gives the message itself without a joining word. el de Valençia, 'he of Valencia'. su[e], the old possessive sue (= su), the e Pidal's (in italics). presentaja, 'gift'.

sentences.t:
Alegre f[o] el rey, non vi[di]estes atanto,
mandó cavalgar apriessa todos sos fijos dalgo
i en los primeros el rey fuera dió salto,
a ve[e]r estos mensajes del que en buen ora nasco.
sentences.l:
Glad wa[s] the king, not you-s[a]w so-much,
he-ordered to-ride in-haste all his sons of-something
and among the first the king outside gave leap,
to s[e]e these messengers of-him who in good hour was-born.
sentences.i: The king was glad — you never saw the like; he ordered all his nobles to mount in haste, and among the first the king himself rode out to see these messengers of him who was born in a good hour.
sentences.n: Tirada 99 (assonance á-o) — The king rides out to receive the Çid's men; Garci Ordóñez's envy (Pidal: El rey sale a recibir a los del Cid. — Envidia de Garci Ordóñez). The line-ends run atanto, dalgo, salto, nasco: stressed á, then o. f[o] = fue, the o Pidal's (in italics). non vi[di]estes atanto, 'you never saw so much', the singer to his hearers; vidiestes = visteis, the di Pidal's (in italics); atanto, 'so much'. mandó cavalgar … todos sos fijos dalgo, 'he ordered all his nobles to ride', the infinitive with its subject after it; fijos dalgo = hidalgos, 'sons of something', men of birth. i, most likely 'and' here (it can also mean 'there'). dió salto, 'sallied out' (as dieron salto at v. 1716). ve[e]r, the old two-syllable veer, the second e Pidal's (in italics). mensajes, 'messengers', not 'messages'. del que en buen ora nasco, 'of him who was born in a good hour', the Çid's formula; nasco, old strong preterite of naçer.

sentences.t:
Ifantes de Carrion, sabet, is açertaron,
e co[m]de don Garcia, [del Çid] so enemigo malo.
A los unos plaze e a los otros va pesando.
sentences.l:
Infantes of Carrion, know-ye, there-themselves happened-to-be,
and cou[n]t don Garcia, [of-the Çid] his enemy evil.
To the some it-pleases and to the others it-goes grieving.
sentences.i: The Infantes of Carrión, you should know, happened to be there, and Count García, the Çid's bitter enemy. Some are pleased, and to others it brings grief.
sentences.n: Ifantes de Carrion, here with one f and without the accent (iffantes, Carrión elsewhere; the print's inconsistencies kept): the young lords of Carrión, sons of its counts. Pidal's note: on the greed that the Çid's presents rouse in the men of Carrión, see v. 1372. sabet, imperative, 'know it', to the hearers. is = i se, the adverb i, 'there' (Latin ibi), with the reflexive se squeezed to -s (as ques, sis, assis): i se açertaron, 'happened to be there' (açertarse, 'to chance to be present'). co[m]de = conde, the m Pidal's (in italics). don Garcia is Garci Ordóñez (v. 1345): Pidal's note refers to his introduction on the count. [del Çid], Pidal's (in italics); so enemigo malo, 'his wicked enemy', so = su. A los unos plaze … a los otros va pesando, 'to some it is pleasing, to others it goes grieving' (pesar a uno, 'to vex someone'), ir + gerund.

sentences.i: They had in sight the men of him who was born in a good hour; they take them for an army, and not for men who come bearing a message; King Alfonso kept crossing himself.
sentences.n: A ojo lo[s] avien, 'they had them in view', the king's party the subject; the object los is named again in los del que en buen ora nasco, 'the men of him born in a good hour'; the s of lo[s] is Pidal's (in italics). cuédanse, 'they think' (cuedar, cuidar). almofalla, 'army, host' (Arabic al-maḥalla, 'the camp'). Pidal's note: ca non, 'y no que', 'and not that' (introduction, p. 84); the king's men, seeing the Çid's from afar, think they look more like an army than plain messengers, though they already knew who they were from the word sent ahead at v. 1828. seíse santiguando, 'was crossing himself', seíe (imperfect of seer, 'to be, sit') with its final e lost before the enclitic se, which belongs with the gerund (santiguarse); Pidal's note: the king 'se hacía cruces', crossed himself over and over in amazement.

sentences.t:
Minaya e Per Vermu[doz] adelante son llegados,
firiéronse a tierra, di[ç]ieron de los cavallos;
antel rey Alfons los inoios fincados,
besan la tierra e los pie[de]s amos:
sentences.l:
Minaya and Per Vermu[doz] forward are arrived,
they-struck-themselves to ground, they-desc[e]nded from the horses;
before-the king Alfons the knees planted,
they-kiss the ground and the fe[e]t both:
sentences.i: Minaya and Per Vermudoz have ridden up ahead; they leapt to the ground, they got down from their horses; kneeling before King Alfonso, they kiss the ground and both his feet:
sentences.n: son llegados, ser + participle with a verb of motion. Pidal's note: firiéronse a tierra, 'echaron pie a tierra', 'they set foot to the ground' (compare vv. 2019, 3025); di[ç]ieron, 'se apearon', 'they dismounted' (v. 1394), from deçir, Latin descendere, the ç Pidal's (in italics). antel = ante el. los inoios fincados, 'the knees planted', a participle clause standing on its own; inoios = inojos, hinojos, 'knees'. pie[de]s, the old plural piedes, the de Pidal's (in italics).

sentences.t:
“Merced, rey Alfonsso, sodes tan ondrado!
por mio Çid el Campeador todo esto vos besamos;
sentences.l:
“Mercy, king Alfonsso, you-are so honoured!
for my Çid the Campeador all this to-you we-kiss;
sentences.i: “Mercy, King Alfonso, honoured as you are! for my Çid the Campeador we give you all these kisses;
sentences.n: The speech is the two messengers' together. Merced, spelled here with plain c (merçed at v. 1351), 'mercy, grace', the petitioner's word. sodes tan ondrado, 'you are so honoured', a courtesy spoken to the king's face; ondrado = honrado. por mio Çid, 'on behalf of my Çid'. todo esto vos besamos, 'all this we kiss you': the ground and the feet they have just kissed.

sentences.t:
a vos llama por señor, e tienes por vuestro vassallo
mucho preçia la ondra el Çid quel avedes dado.
sentences.l:
you he-calls for lord, and he-holds-himself for your vassal
much prizes the honour the Çid that-to-him you-have given.
sentences.i: he calls you his lord and holds himself your vassal; greatly does the Çid prize the honour you have done him.
sentences.n: llamar por señor, 'to call (one's) lord'. tienes = tiene se, 'he holds himself' (tenerse por, 'to count oneself'). Pidal prints no stop at the end of v. 1847. preçia, 'prizes'. la ondra … quel avedes dado, 'the honour that you have given him', quel = que le: the king's release of his wife and daughters (vv. 1350–66, tirada 82). avedes = habéis.

sentences.t:
Pocos días ha, rey, que una lid a arrancado:
a aquel rey de Marruecos, Yúceff por nombrado,
con çincuaenta mill arrancólos del campo.
sentences.l:
Few days it-has, king, that a battle he-has won:
to that king of Marruecos, Yúceff by named,
with fifty thousand he-routed-them from-the field.
sentences.i: It is but a few days, my king, since he won a battle: that king of Morocco, Yúsuf by name, with his fifty thousand, he has driven from the field.
sentences.n: Pocos días ha, 'a few days ago' (ha = hace, aver of time). a arrancado = ha arrancado, 'he has won'. a aquel rey … arrancólos, the personal object with a, picked up again by los: the king and his army. Yúceff, here with ff (Yúcef at v. 1621), Yúsuf, king of Morocco. por nombrado, 'by name'. çincuaenta, so printed here (çinquaenta at vv. 1718 and 1734). arrancólos del campo, 'he routed them off the field'.

sentences.t:
L[o]s ganad[o]s que [fizo] mucho son sobejan[o]s,
ricos son venidos todos los sos vassallos,
e embíavos dozientos cavallos, e bésavos las manos.”
sentences.l:
Th[e] gain[s] that [he-made] much are excessiv[e],
rich are come all the his vassals,
and he-sends-you two-hundred horses, and he-kisses-you the hands.”
sentences.i: The spoils he took are past all measure; all his vassals have grown rich; and he sends you two hundred horses, and kisses your hands.”
sentences.n: L[o]s ganad[o]s … sobejan[o]s: three o's and the word [fizo] are Pidal's (in italics), his mending of the line. Pidal's note: ganados, 'ganancias', 'gains, spoils' (compare v. 481, where gañados takes in sheep, cows and clothing alike), not 'cattle'. mucho son sobejanos, 'are very excessive', beyond measure. ricos son venidos, 'have come to be rich', ser + participle. embíavos = embía vos, 'he sends you'; bésavos las manos, 'he kisses your hands', the formula of homage.

sentences.i: King Alfonso said: “I receive them gladly. I thank my Çid for sending me such a gift; may I yet see the hour when he has cause to be pleased with me.”
sentences.n: Reçíbolos, 'I receive them', the pronoun after the verb at the head of the sentence. de grado, 'gladly'. Gradéscolo, 'I am grateful for it' (gradeçer). don, 'gift'. Pidal's note: aun vea ora que, 'ojalá llegue tiempo que', 'may the time come when' (compare v. 205, where the Çid says it to Martín Antolínez). sea pagado de mí, 'be pleased with me', that is, have good from me: the king now speaks of rewarding the exile.

sentences.t: Esto plogo a muchos e besáronle las manos.
sentences.l: This pleased to many and they-kissed-him the hands.
sentences.i: This pleased many, and they kissed his hands.
sentences.n: plogo, preterite of plazer, 'it pleased'. besáronle las manos, the hand-kiss of thanks; le, the dative of the possessor.

sentences.t:
Pesó al co[m]de don García, e mal era irado;
con diez de s[o]s parientes aparte davan salto:
sentences.l:
It-grieved to-the cou[n]t don García, and badly he-was angered;
with ten of h[i]s kinsmen apart they-were-giving leap:
sentences.i: It grieved Count García, and he was sorely angered; with ten of his kinsmen he drew off to one side:
sentences.n: Pesó al co[m]de, 'it weighed on the count', the m Pidal's (in italics). mal era irado, 'he was badly angered' (irado, 'wrathful'). s[o]s = sus, the o Pidal's (in italics). Pidal's note: aparte davan salto, literally 'salían aparte', 'they went out apart', 'se apartaban para hablar', 'they drew aside to talk'; the plural verb takes in the count and his kin.

sentences.t:
“¡Maravilla es del Çid, que su ondra creçe tanto.
En la ondra que él ha nos seremos abiltados;
sentences.l:
“Marvel it-is of-the Çid, that his honour grows so-much.
In the honour that he has we will-be debased;
sentences.i: “It is a marvel about this Çid, how his honour grows and grows! In the honour he has we shall be shamed;
sentences.n: Maravilla es del Çid, 'it is a wonder about the Çid', said with spite. creçe, 'grows'. ondra = honra. ha, 'has' (aver as full verb). abiltados, 'debased, put to shame' (abiltar, from vil, 'base'): the Çid's rise is the count's fall.

sentences.t:
por tan biltadamientre vençer reyes del campo,
commo si los fallasse muertos aduzirse los cavallos
por esto que él faze nos abremos enbargo.”
sentences.i: for he beats kings in the field so easily, and carries off their horses as if he had found them dead: by what he does we shall come to harm.”
sentences.n: biltadamientre, 'basely', from the same root as abiltados; Pidal's note: 'fácilmente, sin esfuerzo', 'easily, without effort', as if the enemy were worth nothing (Garci Ordóñez's sneer of vv. 1346–47 again). por … vençer, 'for (his) conquering', an infinitive clause. commo si los fallasse muertos, 'as if he found them dead', fallasse = hallase, imperfect subjunctive (f- for h-). aduzirse los cavallos, 'to bring the horses away for himself' (aduzir, 'to bring'). The three verses hang together loosely, as spoken anger does. enbargo, 'hindrance, harm'. abremos, future of aver, 'we will have'.

sentences.t:
Fabló el rey don Alfons [odredes lo que diz]:
“Grado al Criador e a señor sant Esidr[e]
estos dozientos cavallos quem enbía mio Çid.
sentences.l:
Spoke the king don Alfons [you-will-hear that which he-says]:
“Thanks to-the Creator and to lord saint Esidr[e]
these two-hundred horses that-me sends my Çid.
sentences.i: King Alfonso spoke — you shall hear what he says: “Thanks be to the Creator and to my lord Saint Isidore for these two hundred horses my Çid sends me.
sentences.n: Tirada 100 (assonance í) — The king shows himself well disposed toward the Çid (Pidal: El rey muéstrase benévolo hacia el Cid). The line-ends diz, Çid, servir, aquí, vestir carry a stressed í; Esidr[e] counts with them, its unstressed final e disregarded. The second half of v. 1866, odredes lo que diz, is wholly Pidal's (in italics): odredes, the future of oír (= oiréis); diz = dize, 'he says'. Grado, 'thanks'. sant Esidr[e], Saint Isidore of Seville, the king's patron (Pidal's note: v. 1342), the e Pidal's (in italics). estos dozientos cavallos follows on without a preposition: 'thanks … (for) these two hundred horses'. quem = que me.

sentences.t: Mio reyno adelant mejor me podrá servir.
sentences.l: My reign forward better me he-will-be-able to-serve.
sentences.i: From now on in my reign he will be able to serve me better.
sentences.n: Pidal's note: 'en lo sucesivo de mi reinado', 'in the rest of my reign'. adelant = adelante, 'forward, henceforth'. podrá, 'he will be able'. The king speaks of the Çid as a vassal again.

sentences.t:
A vos Minaya Álbar Fáñez e a Per Vermu[doz] aquí
mándovos los cuorpos ondradamientre vestir
e guarnirvos de todas armas commo vos dixiéredes aquí,
que bien parescades ante R[o]y Díaz mio Çid;
sentences.l:
To you Minaya Álbar Fáñez and to Per Vermu[doz] here
I-order-you the bodies honourably to-clothe
and to-furnish-you with all arms as you may-say here,
that well you-may-appear before R[o]y Díaz my Çid;
sentences.i: To you, Minaya Álvar Fáñez, and to Per Vermudoz here: I order you to be clad in honourable dress and furnished with every kind of arms, as you shall ask it here, so that you may make a fine showing before Ruy Díaz, my Çid;
sentences.n: A vos … mándovos, 'to you … I order you', the persons named first and taken up again by vos. los cuorpos … vestir, 'to clothe the bodies', to dress you honourably (cuorpos = cuerpos; ondradamientre, 'honourably', -mientre the adverb ending, = -mente). guarnirvos, 'to equip you'. commo vos dixiéredes, 'as you may say', future subjunctive: 'as you choose'. aquí, 'here', closes vv. 1870, 1872 and 1874 to fill out the í assonance. parescades, present subjunctive of pareçer, 'that you may appear (well)'. R[o]y Díaz, the o Pidal's (in italics).

sentences.t: dovos tres cavallos e prendedlos aquí.
sentences.l: I-give-you three horses and take-them here.
sentences.i: I give you three horses; take them here.
sentences.n: dovos = do vos, 'I give you' (do = doy), the present for a firm gift. prendedlos, imperative + los, 'take them'.

sentences.t:
Assí commo semeja e la veluntad me lo diz,
todas estas nuevas a bien abrán de venir.”
sentences.l:
So as it-seems and the will to-me it says,
all these news to good will-have to come.”
sentences.i: As it seems to me, and as my heart tells me, all these doings will come to good.”
sentences.n: Assí commo semeja, 'as it seems'. veluntad = voluntad, 'will, heart'. me lo diz, 'tells me so'. Pidal's note: nuevas, 'sucesos, negocios', 'events, affairs', not 'news'. a bien abrán de venir, 'will have to come to good', aver de + infinitive for what is bound to happen.

sentences.t:
Besáronle las manos y entraron a posar;
bien los mandó servir de quanto huebos han.
sentences.l:
They-kissed-him the hands and they-entered to lodge;
well them he-ordered to-serve with as-much-as need they-have.
sentences.i: They kissed his hands and went in to their lodging; he gave orders that they be well provided with all they needed.
sentences.n: Tirada 101 (assonance á) — The Infantes of Carrión think of marrying the Çid's daughters (Pidal: Los infantes de Carrión piensan casar con las hijas del Cid). The line-ends posar, han, contar, poridad, adelant carry a stressed á. y, 'and', here so spelled. entraron a posar, 'went in to lodge'. Pidal's note: 'bien los mandó proveer de cuanto necesitaron', 'he had them well supplied with all they needed', as at v. 2639; huebos (v. 123), 'need' (Latin opus): aver huebos, 'to have need of'.

sentences.t:
D' iffantes de Carrión yo vos quiero contar,
fablando en s[o] conssejo, aviendo su poridad:
sentences.l:
Of infantes of Carrión I to-you want to-tell,
speaking in th[ei]r council, having their secret-talk:
sentences.i: Of the Infantes of Carrión I want to tell you now, how they talked in their council, taking secret counsel together:
sentences.n: D' iffantes = de iffantes, 'of the Infantes', the singer turning to his hearers (yo vos quiero contar). s[o] = su, here 'their', the o Pidal's (in italics). conssejo, 'council, deliberation'. poridad, 'secret, private conference' (Latin puritas): aviendo su poridad, 'holding their secret talk'.

sentences.i: “The Çid's affairs go mightily forward; let us ask for his daughters' hands in marriage: we shall grow in honour and go forward ourselves.”
sentences.n: Pidal's note: 'los negocios del Cid prosperan mucho', 'the Çid's affairs prosper greatly'; nuevas again 'affairs, fortunes' (v. 1876). adelant = adelante. demandemos, subjunctive of exhortation, 'let us ask for'. pora con ellas casar, 'in order to marry with them', the infinitive set last. creçremos, future of creçer with the vowel dropped (= creceremos). The Infantes' scheme of tirada 82 (vv. 1372–76), which they then dared not put forward, is now put into action: they too mean to go adelant, 'forward', on the Çid's riches.

sentences.t: Vinien al rey Alfons con esta poridad:
sentences.l: They-were-coming to-the king Alfons with this secret:
sentences.i: They went to King Alfonso with this secret plan:
sentences.n: Vinien, imperfect of venir in -ie (= venían). poridad, 'secret matter'. Their petition to the king is spoken in the next tirada, which opens the following part.
